claims.text: Publicly available large language models hallucinate at least 58% of the time when asked direct, verifiable questions about randomly selected federal court cases.
ChatGPT 4 achieves the lowest mean hallucination rate among tested models at 58% across reference-based legal tasks.
Llama 2 exhibits a mean hallucination rate of 88% across reference-based legal tasks.
Large language model legal hallucination rates decrease as one ascends the judicial hierarchy from district courts to appellate courts to the Supreme Court.
Large language model legal hallucination rates decline sharply for cases exceeding the 90th percentile of legal prominence.
Large language models frequently generate answers that uncritically accept false legal premises embedded in user prompts.
Tested off-the-shelf large language models systematically overestimate their confidence relative to their actual rate of accuracy on legal queries.

evidence.description: Empirical evaluation across reference-based legal queries shows mean hallucination rates ranging from 58% to 88% across GPT-4, GPT-3.5, PaLM 2, and Llama 2.
Pooled reference-based task evaluation yields a 0.58 mean hallucination rate for GPT-4.
Pooled reference-based task evaluation yields a 0.88 mean hallucination rate for Llama 2.
Across all models, hallucination rates are lowest for SCOTUS cases, higher for USCOA cases, and highest for USDC cases.
Analysis of SCOTUS cases by PageRank percentile score demonstrates a sharp decrease in mean hallucination rate around the 90th percentile score for GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and PaLM 2.
On contra-factual tasks, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and PaLM 2 hallucinated answers to false dissenting and false overruling premises instead of rejecting the premise.

Expected calibration error (ECE) measurements across reference-based tasks demonstrate positive calibration error, indicating models overestimate confidence relative to actual non-hallucination rates.

methodologies.name: Reference-based Legal Question Answering Evaluation
methodologies.description: An evaluation framework comparing deterministic model responses against tabular ground-truth legal metadata for factual legal tasks.
datasets: Library of Congress Overruled Decisions Table

methodologies.name: Reference-free Contradiction-based Hallucination Detection
methodologies.description: A method to establish a lower bound on hallucination rates by querying an LLM twice at temperature tau = 1 and using GPT-4 to identify logical self-contradictions.

limitations.text: The reference-free contradiction detection methodology provides only a lower bound on hallucination rates because two responses can be logically consistent yet still factually incorrect.
The contradiction evaluation approach cannot identify repeated, consistent false statements generated across stochastic calls as hallucinations.
Prior research on legal LLM hallucinations focused on closed-domain tasks like summarizing judicial opinions or synthesizing provided text rather than open-domain legal retrieval.

future_work.text: Developing legal hallucination benchmarks to evaluate open-domain legal factual consistency across evolving large language models.
Exploring technical and normative trade-offs when optimizing legal models between prompt fidelity, corpus fidelity, and real-world factuality.
